criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to, uptake of, and affordability of pit latrine emptying and fecal sludge management (FSM) sanitation services in dense informal settlements of Kigali, Rwanda.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 ('institutional ... factor') but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the literal/plain broad wording, the study touches on institutional service-delivery factors by testing consumer preferences for formalized/registered business provision versus informal day laborers ('Formality of services'), commercial pricing formats (volumetric vs. flat-fee charges and group-aggregation discounts), and a survey covariate for whether the resident household versus the landlord is responsible for pit maintenance costs. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, however, none of the empirically studied exposures is a legal, administrative, regulatory, or utility tariff/governance rule directly governing service access: Pit Vidura is a private social enterprise operating in an unregulated private market, the revealed-preference trial varies promotional marketing coupon prices and group discounts, the stated-preference experiment measures consumer willingness to pay for service quality/branding attributes, the cost model estimates truck operational scale economies, the landlord-responsibility variable is merely an unanalysed payer control in coupon uptake regressions (without examining tenancy law, documentation, or tenure rules), and municipal cross-subsidy surcharges or forthcoming pit-sealing bans are mentioned only as unstudied background or hypothetical policy recommendations.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical evidence from a cluster-randomized coupon pricing trial and baseline survey of 1,167 households across 30 villages (N = 1,176-1,179 in logistic regressions including neighbor group-empty participants), a stated-preference discrete choice survey of 157 households/landlords analyzed via multinomial logit, and primary operational expense accounting from Pit Vidura service records.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household requests/uptake of improved pit-emptying services, forecasted coverage/demand across price levels (affordability and exclusion of low-income households at full-cost-recovery prices), and willingness to pay (WTP) relative to unit delivery costs.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the household/landlord population and unit of analysis (households in 30 villages across 10 sectors in Kigali), the economic/operational exposures, the service uptake and WTP outcomes, and the empirical study designs.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study is a gap analysis between the WTP and the cost of service delivery for improved, formalized FS collection, operating in Kigali, Rwanda. Pit Vidura is a social enterprise that delivers formalized, improved pit latrine emptying and FS transport services to low-income households in informal settlements in Kigali.

evidence_quotes.quote: Each village was randomly assigned one type of coupon, and all of the participants in that village received the same coupon. Each coupon included a volumetric price for an individual empty, as well as a volumetric discount for a group empty
Services provided by a branded, registered business, with workers wearing uniforms and using protective gear
whether the household was solely or partially responsible for pit maintenance (vs. if the landlord was solely responsible) and a categorical variable of reported pit fullness

While most governments provide heavy subsidies for storm water drainage, sewerage, and even wastewater treatment where it exists, the regulation, oversight, investment, and subsidy of FS management have been limited. Services are almost always provided by the private sector, and often by informal operators.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 5 of 18 (Section 2.3. Stated Preference Study Design)
evidence_quotes.quote: We conducted a stated preference survey of WTP for improved pit emptying services, while using a discrete choice framework, during our follow-up surveys of households and landlords.

Our results show that, at a price of US$79 per pit, 15% of all the pits would be emptied by improved emptying services, roughly the current rate of manual emptying. Grouping empties by neighborhood and ensuring that each truck services an average of four households per day could reduce the production costs to US$44 per empty, ensuring full cost coverage at that price.

raw_response.exposure: Randomly assigned promotional coupon volumetric prices and group-empty discounts for a private social enterprise's (Pit Vidura) pit-emptying service; household vs. landlord responsibility for pit maintenance costs and pit fullness; stated-preference service attributes (price, flat fee vs. volumetric pricing, branded/registered business with worker protective gear vs. informal laborers, sludge treatment, distant disposal, response speed, pre-full group emptying, pit sealing); and operational truck capacity/scale (rented flatbed vs. owned exhauster truck at 1-4 empties/day)
raw_response.outcome: Household requests/uptake of formalized individual and group pit-latrine emptying services, willingness to pay (WTP) for emptying service attributes, operational cost per empty, and the cost-recovery/affordability gap
raw_response.population_and_sample: Low-income households with pit latrines across 30 villages in 10 dense informal-settlement sectors of Kigali, Rwanda (N = 1,167 coupon-receiving households in baseline Survey 1, plus 12 neighbor households in group empties; N = 157 households/landlords in follow-up Survey 2/3 discrete choice survey)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Although the paper empirically examines household sanitation service uptake and affordability (pit latrine emptying in informal settlements of Kigali, Rwanda), its empirical exposures are market willingness-to-pay attributes, promotional coupon price levels and group-empty discounts offered by an unregulated private social enterprise (Pit Vidura), and operational truck-scale cost scenarios rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, or public-utility tariff/governance rule directly governing service access. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it examines consumer valuation of formalized/registered enterprise delivery versus informal day laborers, volumetric versus flat-fee pricing formats, and a covariate for household versus landlord financial responsibility for pit maintenance; however, none of these constitutes an analyzed rule-type legal or administrative mechanism under the active 2026-10-13 scope clarification (and municipal cross-subsidy surcharges or forthcoming sealing bans are discussed only hypothetically or as unmeasured context).
raw_response.study_design: Cluster-randomized revealed-preference coupon pricing trial, stated-preference discrete choice experiment, and operational cost modeling
